mentions.text: I agree Nike style is the right move. The caveat is that we used to have a liquid and legible labor market for pricing and allocating computer talent. This is in flux now. I think if you want to keep working in computer technology you need some more chutzpah than was required a decade ago. “Grind Leetcode and spam job boards” won’t get you far these days. It’s better to network, make durable relationships, focus on solving persistent and novel problems. We have to be real engineers once more instead lavishly remunerated corporate monkeys.

mentions.text: > about the economy and AI. This is true for any economy, not just AI and the central contradiction of capitalism. Automation raises profits for a brief moment until everyone else has caught up. Once the new profit margin equalizes across an industry, competition sets in and margins shrink. To keep margins up, labour costs need to fall further. That is why companies like Nike or Adidas produce in low-income countries. The investments in automation is such that profits can only be maintained through mass production, low wages, long working hours and raised demand through brand lock-in, classic marketing. The current open bet is that equalization of AI technology can't be achieved across industries because of the important entry barrier: capital and compute. Monopolization should hold long enough to make the rest of the world market dependent on US AI infrastructure. The rest will feel the devaluation of their work, they will get poorer - some straight away, some indirectly because of the shrinking customer base.
